paper.title: Mechanistic insights into state-dependent synchronization of neural activity by weak tACS fields
paper.abstract: Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) biases spike timing with weak electric fields, but how recurrent circuitry and network state shape this response is unclear. We simulated tACS in a detailed cortical column model in two network states of varying coherence, roughly corresponding to REM-like and NREM-like states. Despite weak impacts on network firing rates, stimulation entrained network activity at realistically occurring field strengths. Global entrainment was initiated by direct entrainment of ongoing pyramidal cell activity, which subsequently recruited inhibitory interneurons in a state-dependent manner. The NREM-like network locked more strongly to all tested stimulation frequencies, independent of baseline spectral power, and displayed larger recurrent-connectivity-mediated phase lags. However, recurrent connectivity was not required for, and did not amplify, entrainment, but instead produced an offset in baseline network activity. Our results highlight the impact of network state on the response to tACS, and suggest that meso-scale models of electromagnetic-electrophysiological interactions must look beyond single-cell polarization and baseline oscillations at the stimulation frequency.

paper.title: Self-organized fractional silencing of pyramidal neurons under global depolarization in a spatial neuron-glial microcircuit model
paper.abstract: Pathological transitions in nervous tissue, including epileptiform discharges and cortical spreading depolarization, depend on the interplay between cellular and interstitial mechanisms. We develop a biophysically detailed two-dimensional model of the neurogliovascular unit (NGVU) integrating neuronal populations in the Hodgkin-Huxley formalism, astrocyte-regulated extracellular potassium dynamics, extracellular neurotransmitter spillover, and noradrenergic neuromodulation. Numerical simulations show that inhibitory interneurons enter depolarization block (DB) at significantly lower extracellular potassium concentrations and stimulation intensities than pyramidal neurons. Early loss of inhibition shifts the local excitation-inhibition balance and triggers network hyperexcitability. In the spatially extended network, exceeding a critical stimulation threshold induces a transition from heterogeneous but spatially uniform firing to network fragmentation into stable active microclusters with self-sustained high-frequency firing. Pyramidal neurons with lower excitatory synaptic input receive less recurrent excitation, which protects them from DB. By continuously releasing potassium ions and glutamate into the extracellular space, pyramidal neurons drive strong depolarization in more densely connected neighbors and push them into deep DB. Simulations of localized astrocytic dysfunction predict a spatial limit for potassium clearance defects. Small damaged cores are fully compensated by diffusion and uptake by surrounding healthy astrocyte units. However, above a critical damage size, activity-dependent potassium buildup and firing positive feedback disrupt homeostasis in surrounding units, promoting persistent depolarized centers with self-sustained, spatially segregated pathological activity.

paper.title: Spatial model of neurogliovascular unit: arachidonic acid can control the stability
paper.abstract: Arachidonic acid metabolites can have both vasoconstrictor and vasodilator effects, thereby influencing neuronal activity. In this work, to analyze possible patterns of activity of nervous tissue in response to changes in the metabolic profile, a mathematical model of a spatially distributed system of connected neurogliovascular units was developed. We simulate the influence of arachidonic acid metabolites on the dynamics of the neurogliovascular unit during cortical spreading depression in order to determine the ways in which astrocytic activity influences the spatiotemporal characteristics of the propagating cortical depression wave. It is assumed that in the future the results of the theoretical study can be used to find ways to remove nervous tissue from pathological conditions that occur in epilepsy, migraines and a number of neurodegenerative diseases, including those associated with the occurrence of cortical depression waves.
